🤖 Meta AI

28/06/24, 11:31 am

The warnings you're seeing are related to Git's handling of line endings. By default, Git converts line endings from CRLF (Windows style) to LF (Unix style) when committing changes. This is because most version control systems, including Git, were originally designed for Unix-like systems, which use LF as the line ending character.

To retain LF line endings and avoid the warnings, you can try the following:

  1. Set core.autocrlf to input (which you've already done):
bash
git config --global core.autocrlf input

This will tell Git to only convert line endings when committing changes, but not when checking out files.

  1. Set core.eol to lf (this will override the core.autocrlf setting):
bash
git config --global core.eol lf

This will tell Git to always use LF as the line ending character, even on Windows.

  1. Add the following line to your .gitattributes file (create one if it doesn't exist):
* text eol=lf

This will tell Git to use LF as the line ending character for all text files.

After making these changes, try running git add . again to see if the warnings persist. If they do, you can try resetting the Git repository using git reset --hard and then re-adding your changes.

Remember that changing the line ending settings can affect how your files are displayed in different environments, so make sure you're aware of the implications.

🤖 Meta AI

03/07/24, 5:54 pm

You can use the following regular expression pattern with grep:

^admin\s{3}\d{5}.*

Here's a breakdown of how it works:

  • ^ matches the start of the line
  • admin matches the string "admin" literally
  • \s{3} matches exactly 3 whitespace characters (spaces or tabs)
  • \d{5} matches exactly 5 digits
  • .* matches any characters (including none) until the end of the line, but since it's not included in the match, it won't be part of the output.

Note: The {3} and {5} are quantifiers that specify the exact number of spaces and digits to match, respectively.

You can use this pattern with grep like this:

grep -E '^admin\s{3}\d{5}.*' filename

The -E option enables extended regular expressions, which allows us to use {3} and {5} quantifiers.

The issue is that you haven't set a default Rust version. Rustup allows you to install and manage multiple versions of Rust, but you need to specify which one to use as the default.

To fix this, run the following command:

rustup default stable

This will download and set the latest stable version of Rust as your default toolchain. After running this command, you should be able to use the rustc command without any issues.

Also, make sure to source the rustup env file in your shell configuration file (~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile) to set the PATH environment variable correctly. Add the following line to your shell config file:

source /opt/rustup/env

Then, restart your shell or run source ~/.bashrc to apply the changes.

That should fix the issue!

To convert decimal hours to Unix timestamps (integer seconds) in Python, you can use the following approach:

import math

# Example data
decimal_hours = [0.547476852, 0.547476852, 0.548599537, 0.548599537, 0.548599537, 0.553460648, 0.550115741]

# Convert decimal hours to Unix timestamps (integer seconds)
unix_timestamps = [math.floor(decimal_hour * 3600) for decimal_hour in decimal_hours]

print(unix_timestamps)

This code uses a list comprehension to iterate over the decimal hours, multiplies each value by 3600 (to convert hours to seconds), and then uses the math.floor function to truncate the decimal part, effectively converting the values to integers.

[1973, 1973, 1977, 1977, 1977, 2004, 1983]

To fix this, you can modify your UDF to handle both cases: when timestamps is a list of lists and when it's a single float value. Here's an updated version of your UDF:

from datetime import datetime
import xlwings as xw

@xw.func
def convert_timestamps_decimals(timestamps):
    if isinstance(timestamps, list):  # Check if timestamps is a list
        converted_dates = []
        for row in timestamps:
            converted_row = []
            for timestamp in row:
                timestamp_seconds = timestamp * 86400
                dt_object = datetime.fromtimestamp(timestamp_seconds)
                date_string = dt_object.strftime('%d/%m/%Y')
                converted_row.append(date_string)
            converted_dates.append(converted_row)
    else:  # If timestamps is not a list, assume it's a single float value
        timestamp_seconds = timestamps * 86400
        dt_object = datetime.fromtimestamp(timestamp_seconds)
        converted_dates = dt_object.strftime('%d/%m/%Y')
    return converted_dates

This updated UDF checks if timestamps is a list using isinstance(timestamps, list). If it is, it processes the data as before. If not, it assumes timestamps is a single float value and converts it directly to a date string.

Please note that this updated UDF returns a list of lists when timestamps is a list of lists, and a single string when timestamps is a float. If you need a different behavior, adjust the return statements accordingly.

08/07/24, 12:22 pm

The issue with your regex pattern is that the .* in (?<=^\().*(?=NSE.*$) is greedy, meaning it matches as many characters as possible. To fix this, you can make the .* lazy by adding a ? after it, like this: (?<=^\()(.*?)NSE.*$

Here's a breakdown of the corrected pattern:

  • (?<=^\() : Positive lookbehind to match the opening parenthesis at the start of the string
  • (.*?) : Capture group to match any characters (lazily, thanks to the ?) until...
  • NSE : the string "NSE" is matched
  • .*$ : any remaining characters until the end of the string

By making the .* lazy, the capture group will stop matching as soon as it encounters "NSE", rather than matching the entire string.

Here's a Python code snippet to demonstrate the corrected pattern:

import re

s = "(BAJAJ-AUTO NSE) BAJAJ AUTO LTD."
pattern = r'(?<=^\()(.*?)NSE.*$'
match = re.search(pattern, s)
if match:
    print(match.group(1))  # prints "BAJAJ-AUTO"

  • (?<=^\() : Positive lookbehind to match the opening parenthesis at the start of the string
  • (.*?) : Capture group to match any characters (lazily, thanks to the ?) until...
  • (?=\)) : Positive lookahead to match the closing parenthesis

This pattern will match only the text within the parentheses, excluding the parentheses themselves and any other characters outside them.

Here's a Python code snippet to demonstrate the corrected pattern:

s = "(BAJAJ-AUTO NSE) BAJAJ AUTO LTD."
pattern = r'(?<=^\()(.*?)(?=\))'

Difference between ".?" and "."?

🤖 Meta AI

08/07/24, 12:58 pm

In regular expressions, .* and .*? are both greedy and lazy matchers, respectively, for any characters (including none). The key difference lies in their behavior:

.* (Greedy):

  • Matches as many characters as possible (including none)
  • Tries to match the longest possible string

.*? (Lazy):

  • Matches as few characters as possible (including none)
  • Tries to match the shortest possible string

In other words, the greedy matcher (.*) will try to match as much as it can, while the lazy matcher (.*?) will try to match as little as it can.

For example, consider the string "abc":

  • .* will match the entire string "abc"
  • .*? will match an empty string, since it matches as few characters as possible

In the context of the regex pattern I provided earlier, (?<=^\()(.*?)(?=\)), the lazy matcher .*? is used to match the text within the parentheses, stopping as soon as it encounters the closing parenthesis. If we used the greedy matcher .* instead, it would match too much, including the closing parenthesis and any subsequent characters.

To avoid these warnings and ensure that Git doesn't replace CRLF with LF, you can configure Git to respect the line endings in your files. Here are a few steps to help you achieve this:

  1. Check your Git configuration: Run the command git config core.autocrlf to see your current configuration. If it's set to input or true, Git will convert CRLF to LF.
  2. Set core.autocrlf to false: Run the command git config --global core.autocrlf false to tell Git to respect the line endings in your files and not convert them.
  3. Reset your Git repository: Run the command git reset --hard to reset your repository to its previous state, before you ran git add ..
  4. Add your files again: Run the command git add . to stage your changes again, but this time, Git should respect the line endings in your files.

By following these steps, you should be able to avoid the warnings and ensure that Git doesn't replace CRLF with LF in your files.

The issue you're encountering is due to the fact that the ^ character in a regular expression matches the start of a string, but in your case, the string is the entire cell value, not just the visible text. The tab character is not included in the string, so the pattern ^\W doesn't match.

To fix this, you can use the re.match function instead of re.search, which matches the pattern at the beginning of the string. Also, you need to include the tab character in the pattern. You can do this by using \t in the pattern.

Here's the updated code:

import xlwings as xw
import re

@xw.func
@xw.arg('excel_range', ndim=2)
@xw.arg('patterns', ndim=1)
def REGEXFINDM(excel_range, patterns):
    result = []
    for row in excel_range:
        row_result = []
        for cell in row:
            cell_str = str(cell)  # Convert cell to string
            cell_result = []
            for pattern in patterns:
                match = re.match(pattern, cell_str)
                if match:
                    cell_result.append(cell_str)  # Return the entire string
            if len(cell_result) == len(patterns):
                row_result.append(" ".join(cell_result))
            else:
                row_result.append("")
        result.append(row_result)
    return result

And then use the UDF like this:

=IF(REGEXFINDM(S5,"^\t\W")="",TRUE,FALSE)

This should correctly identify cells that start with a tab character followed by a non-word character.

Here's the updated code:

import xlwings as xw
import re

@xw.func
@xw.arg('excel_range', ndim=2)
@xw.arg('patterns', ndim=1)
def REGEXFINDM(excel_range, patterns):
    result = []
    for row in excel_range:
        row_result = []
        for cell in row:
            cell_str = str(cell)  # Convert cell to string
            cell_result = []
            for pattern in patterns:
                match = re.search(pattern, cell_str, flags=re.UNICODE)
                if match:
                    cell_result.append(cell_str)  # Return the entire string
            if len(cell_result) == len(patterns):
                row_result.append(" ".join(cell_result))
            else:
                row_result.append("")
        result.append(row_result)
    return result

And then use the UDF like this:

import xlwings as xw
import re

@xw.func
@xw.arg('excel_range', ndim=2)
@xw.arg('patterns', ndim=1)
def REGEXFINDM(excel_range, patterns):
    result = []
    for row in excel_range:
        row_result = []
        for cell in row:
            cell_str = str(cell)  # Convert cell to string
            row_result.append(any(re.match(pattern, cell_str, flags=re.UNICODE) for pattern in patterns))
        result.append(row_result)

I apologize for the issue. It seems like there's a limitation with xlwings when returning a dynamic array from a UDF.

As a workaround, you can modify the UDF to return a string with the results separated by a delimiter, and then use Excel's TEXTSPLIT function (available in Excel 2021 and later) to split the string into an array.

Here's the updated code:

import xlwings as xw
import re

@xw.func
@xw.arg('excel_range', ndim=2)
@xw.arg('patterns', ndim=1)
def REGEXFINDM(excel_range, patterns):
    result = []
    for row in excel_range:
        row_result = []
        for cell in row:
            cell_str = str(cell)  # Convert cell to string
            row_result.append('T' if any(re.match(pattern, cell_str, flags=re.UNICODE) for pattern in patterns) else 'F')
        result.append(','.join(row_result))
    return '\n'.join(result)

And then use the UDF like this:

=TEXTSPLIT(REGEXFINDM(S5:S7, {"^\p{C}"}), ",")

This will return a dynamic array with T (True) or F (False) values indicating whether each cell starts with a non-printable character.

Note: If you're using an earlier version of Excel without TEXTSPLIT, you can use other workarounds like using a helper column or a different UDF approach.

  1. git pull origin main - This will fetch the latest changes from the remote repository and merge them with your local changes.
  2. git merge origin/main - This will merge the remote changes with your local changes.
  3. git push origin main - This will push your updated local changes to the remote repository.

Alternatively, you can use git pull --rebase origin main instead of git pull origin main and git merge origin/main. This will replay your local changes on top of the remote changes.

If you want to override the remote repository with your local changes, you can use git push origin main --force. However, use this with caution as it will overwrite the remote repository without merging the changes.

Remember to commit your changes before pushing to the remote repository.

  1. Open Excel
  2. Go to File > Options > Trust Center
  3. Click on "Trust Center Settings"
  4. In the Trust Center Settings dialog, click on "Macro Settings"
  5. Check the box next to "Trust access to the VBA project object model"
  6. Click OK to close the dialog

After enabling this setting, try running your Python script again. The VBA code should now be able to access the VBProject object without errors.

Note: Be aware that enabling this setting can pose a security risk if you open Excel files from untrusted sources, as it allows macros to access the VBA project object model.

Here's a clear differentiation between SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS:

Software as a Service (SaaS)

  • Provides software applications over the internet
  • Users access software via a web browser or app
  • No installation, maintenance, or updates required
  • Examples: Microsoft Office 365, Salesforce, Dropbox

Platform as a Service (PaaS)

  • Provides a complete platform for developing, running, and managing applications
  • Includes tools, libraries, and infrastructure for app development
  • Users control application configuration and data
  • Examples: Heroku, Google App Engine, Microsoft Azure

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)

  • Provides virtualized computing resources over the internet
  • Users control OS, storage, networking, and security
  • Users are responsible for maintenance, updates, and configuration
  • Examples: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, Google Compute Engine

In summary:

  • SaaS provides software applications
  • PaaS provides a platform for app development and deployment
  • IaaS provides virtualized computing resources for users to manage

Think of it like a restaurant:

  • SaaS is like ordering takeout (software is served to you)
  • PaaS is like a kitchen rental (you cook and serve your own food)
  • IaaS is like buying ingredients and cooking at home (you control everything)

In that case, you're dealing with a DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) manifest, which is a playlist file that contains links to the actual video segments. To download the video using FFmpeg, you can use the following options:

  1. -i specifies the input URL (the manifest file)
  2. -c copy copies the original audio and video streams without re-encoding
  3. -bsf specifies the bitstream filter to use (in this case, dash to handle the DASH manifest)

Here's an updated command:

ffmpeg -i "long_url_here" -c copy -bsf dash -b:v 1200k -b:a 192k -s 1366x768 output.mp4

This command will download the video segments from the manifest and concatenate them into a single output file (output.mp4). The -bsf dash option tells FFmpeg to handle the DASH manifest.

If you want to specify a different format for the output file, you can change the container format (e.g., -f mkv for Matroska) and adjust the codecs accordingly.

Keep in mind that the video quality and resolution may vary depending on the available streams in the manifest. You can use the -map option to select a specific stream from the manifest if needed.

Also, be aware that downloading copyrighted content without permission may violate terms of service or copyright laws. Always ensure you have the necessary permissions or rights to download and use the content.

import sympy as sp
import numpy as np

def indefintegral(func_list):
    x = sp.symbols('x')
    result = []
    for func in func_list:
        func = func.replace(' ', '').lower()
        func = sp.sympify(func)
        integral = sp.integrate(func, x)
        result.append(str(integral))
    return result

def defintegral(func_list, lower_limit, upper_limit):
    x = sp.symbols('x')
    result = []
    for func in func_list:
        func = func.replace(' ', '').lower()
        func = sp.sympify(func)
        integral = sp.integrate(func, (x, lower_limit, upper_limit))
        result.append(float(integral))
    return result

The indefintegral function calculates the indefinite integral of each function in the input list. It uses the sympy library to parse the input functions and calculate the integrals.

The defintegral function calculates the definite integral of each function in the input list over the specified range. It also uses sympy to parse the input functions and calculate the integrals.

Note that the input functions should be strings, and the variables should be 'x' (case insensitive). Also, the defintegral function assumes that the input functions are valid and can be integrated over the specified range.

Here's a step-by-step guide on how to access a DLL function from VBA, define it as a custom function, and return an array:

Step 1: Declare the DLL function in VBA

Open the Visual Basic Editor in Excel (Press Alt+F11 or navigate to Developer > Visual Basic). In the code module, declare the DLL function using the Declare statement:

Declare Function MyDllFunction Lib "MyDll.dll" (ByVal arg1 As Long, ByVal arg2 As Long) As Long()

Replace "MyDll.dll" with the actual name of your DLL file, and MyDllFunction with the actual name of the function you want to call. The arguments arg1 and arg2 should match the data types and number of arguments expected by the DLL function.

Step 2: Define the VBA custom function

Create a new VBA function that will wrap the DLL function call:

Public Function MyVbaFunction(arg1 As Long, arg2 As Long) As Variant
    Dim result() As Long
    result = MyDllFunction(arg1, arg2)
    MyVbaFunction = result
End Function

This function takes the same arguments as the DLL function and returns a Variant array.

Step 3: Call the VBA custom function from Excel

In an Excel worksheet, enter the following formula:

excel
=MyVbaFunction(A1, B1)

Assuming A1 and B1 contain the values you want to pass as arguments. Press Enter to execute the formula.

Step 4: Handle the array return value

Since the VBA function returns an array, Excel will display the result as a single cell with the value "{...}". To display the array values, select the cell and go to the "Formulas" tab > "Formula Auditing" > "Evaluate Formula". This will show you the individual array values.

Alternatively, you can use the INDEX function to access individual array elements:

excel
=INDEX(MyVbaFunction(A1, B1), 1)

Replace 1 with the index of the array element you want to access.

That's it! You should now be able to call the DLL function from VBA, pass arguments from Excel, and return an array value.

🤖 Meta AI

08/08/24, 4:46 pm

In Stellarium, the J2000 standard refers to a specific epoch and reference frame for celestial coordinates, not directly related to date and time.

J2000 is a standard epoch for astronomical coordinates, which means it's a fixed moment in time used as a reference point for measuring celestial positions. In this case, J2000 corresponds to January 1, 2000, 12:00 TT (Terrestrial Time).

In Stellarium, the J2000 standard is used for:

  1. Equatorial coordinates (right ascension and declination): These coordinates are fixed relative to the J2000 epoch and are not affected by the date and time.
  2. Ecliptic coordinates (longitude and latitude): These coordinates are also fixed relative to the J2000 epoch and are not affected by the date and time.

When you set the date and time in Stellarium, it will update the planetary positions and other dynamic objects according to the new date and time. However, the J2000 standard remains the reference frame for celestial coordinates.

So, to summarize:

  • J2000 is a standard epoch for celestial coordinates (not directly related to date and time).
  • Date and time in Stellarium control the dynamic positions of objects (e.g., planets, stars).
  • J2000 coordinates remain fixed, regardless of the date and time set in Stellarium.

// Get Sun and Moon's J2000 ecliptic longitudes

// Set the date, time, and location
var date = new Date(2024, 7, 8, 16, 30, 0); // August 8, 2024, 16:30:00
var lon = 77.1025; // East longitude (positive)
var lat = 28.7041; // North latitude (positive)

// Set the observer's location
core.setObserverLocation(lon, lat, 0, 0, 0);

// Set the date and time
core.setDate(date);

// Get the Sun's J2000 ecliptic longitude
var sun = core.getObjectByName("Sun");
var sunEclipticLon = sun.getJ2000EclipticLon();

// Get the Moon's J2000 ecliptic longitude
var moon = core.getObjectByName("Moon");
var moonEclipticLon = moon.getJ2000EclipticLon();

// Print the results
core.debug("Sun's J2000 ecliptic longitude: " + sunEclipticLon);
core.debug("Moon's J2000 ecliptic longitude: " + moonEclipticLon);

This script sets the date, time, and location, and then uses the getJ2000EclipticLon() method to get the J2000 ecliptic longitudes of the Sun and Moon. The results are printed to the console using core.debug().

Note: Make sure to adjust the date, time, and location to your desired values. Also, this script assumes that the Sun and Moon are visible in the sky at the specified date, time, and location.

The issue arises because rng2 is a single-cell range (L14), while rng1 is a multi-cell range (I14:K14). To fix this, you can modify the function to handle single-cell ranges by repeating the value to match the dimensions of the other range. Here's an updated version of the function:

import xlwings as xw

@xw.func
@xw.arg('rng1', ndim=2)
@xw.arg('rng2', ndim=2)
def tstrangecalc(rng1, rng2):
    # Convert single-cell ranges to 2D lists
    if not isinstance(rng1[0], list):
        rng1 = [[rng1[0][0]]]
    if not isinstance(rng2[0], list):
        rng2 = [[rng2[0][0]] * len(rng1[0])]  # Repeat the value to match dimensions

    # Check if the dimensions are the same
    if len(rng1) != len(rng2) or len(rng1[0]) != len(rng2[0]):
        return "#DIMENSION_ERROR"

    # Perform element-wise addition
    result = [[rng1[i][j] + rng2[i][j] for j in range(len(rng1[0]))] for i in range(len(rng1))]
    return result

In this updated version, I added a line to repeat the value in rng2 to match the number of columns in rng1. This should fix the issue when passing a single-cell range as rng2.

Yes, you can use the TEXTSPLIT function, which is available in Excel 365, to split the concatenated string into a dynamic array. Here's how you can do it:

=TEXTSPLIT(G14&H14&I14, " ")

This will split the concatenated string into an array using space as the delimiter. If you want to use a different delimiter, you can replace the space with the desired character.

Alternatively, you can use the TEXTSPLIT function with the FILTERXML function to split the string into an array without using a delimiter:

=FILTERXML("<t><v>" & TEXTJOIN("</v><v>", TRUE, G14, H14, I14) & "</v></t>", "//v")

This will create an XML string with each value wrapped in a <v> tag, and then use FILTERXML to extract the values into an array.

Note that both of these methods will return a dynamic array, which can be used in various Excel functions and formulas.

10/08/24, 10:17 am

The error you're encountering is due to a change in the way CFFI handles DLL loading on Windows.

In the latest version of CFFI, the dlopen function has been updated to use the LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS flag by default, which prevents loading DLLs from the current working directory.

To resolve this issue, you can try one of the following solutions:

  1. Use an absolute path to load the DLL:
C = ffi.dlopen(r'D:\OneDrive - 0yt2k\Compiled dlls & executables\rdrand_multithreaded_new.dll')

  1. Add the directory containing the DLL to the system's PATH environment variable.

  2. Use the ffi.dlopen function with the ffi.RTLD_DEFAULT flag:

C = ffi.dlopen('rdrand_multithreaded_new.dll', ffi.RTLD_DEFAULT)

Regarding the types defined in your C code, they look correct. However, ensure that the types used in your CFFI cdef block match the types used in your C code.

For example, the rdrand64_step function takes an unsigned long long* as an argument, so the CFFI cdef block should define it as:

ffi.cdef("""
    int rdrand64_step(unsigned long long *rand);
""")

Similarly, the generate_random_numbers function takes two int arguments, and the get_numbers function returns an unsigned long long*, so the CFFI cdef block should define them accordingly.

To replace core.debug with core.output, you can simply change the last three lines of your script to:

This will print the same information to the console, but using the core.output function instead of core.debug.

10/08/24, 4:25 pm

Yes, it is possible to run the Stellarium script from xlwings using Python UDF and get Sun and Moon's parameters directly in Excel. You can use the os library to run the script from Python and capture the output.

Here's an example of how you can modify your UDF to run the script and get the output:

import xlwings as xw
import os

@xw.func
def calculate_tithi_excel_new(date):
    # Run the Stellarium script using curl
    cmd = f'curl -d "id=myScript.ssc" http://localhost:8090/api/scripts/run'
    output = os.popen(cmd).read()

    # Parse the output to extract Sun and Moon's parameters
    lines = output.splitlines()
    sun_longitude = None
    moon_longitude = None
    for line in lines:
        if 'Sun:' in line:
            sun_longitude = float(line.split('=')[1])
        elif 'Moon:' in line:
            moon_longitude = float(line.split('=')[1])

    # Calculate the tithi number and name
    longitude_difference = moon_longitude - sun_longitude
    if longitude_difference < 0:
        longitude_difference += 360
    tithi_number = int(longitude_difference // 12) + 1
    paksha = 'Shukla' if tithi_number <= 15 else 'Krishna'
    tithi_names = ['Pratipada', 'Dwitiya', 'Tritiya', 'Chaturthi', 'Panchami', 'Shashthi', 'Saptami', 'Ashtami', 'Navami', 'Dashami', 'Ekadashi', 'Dwadashi', 'Trayodashi', 'Chaturdashi', 'Purnima', 'Amavasya']
    tithi_index = (tithi_number - 1) % 15
    tithi_name = tithi_names[tithi_index]

    return f"{paksha} {tithi_name}"

This UDF runs the Stellarium script using curl, captures the output, extracts the Sun and Moon's parameters, calculates the tithi number and name, and returns the result. Note that you need to replace myScript.ssc with the actual name of your Stellarium script file.

import os

This way, you can keep the script path separate and avoid hardcoding it in the command.

This will pass the script ID myScript.ssc to the Stellarium server, which will then run the corresponding script.

import xlwings as xw
import datetime
import os
import json

# Excel UDF to calculate tithi
@xw.func
def calculate_tithi(date_input):
    # Convert Excel date to datetime object
    date_as_datetime = datetime.datetime.fromordinal(int(date_input) + 693594)

    # Format datetime object as string
    date_string = date_as_datetime.strftime("%d/%m/%Y %H:%M:%S")

    # Replace date string in sun-moon-elongj2000.ssc file
    with open("sun-moon-elongj2000.ssc", "r") as file:
        lines = file.readlines()

    lines[5] = f'var date1 = "{date_string}";\n'

    with open("sun-moon-elongj2000.ssc", "w") as file:
        file.writelines(lines)

    # Run curl command
    os.system('curl -d "id=sun-moon-elongj2000.ssc" http://localhost:8090/api/scripts/run')

    # Parse JSON string from sun-moon.txt file
    with open("C:\\Users\\dhawal123\\AppData\\Roaming\\Stellarium\\sun-moon.txt", "r") as file:
        json_string = file.read()

    data = json.loads(json_string)

    # Extract Sun and Moon's parameters
    sun_longitude = data["Sun"]["elongJ2000"]
    moon_longitude = data["Moon"]["elongJ2000"]

    # Calculate tithi number and name
    longitude_difference = moon_longitude - sun_longitude
    if longitude_difference < 0:
        longitude_difference += 360
    tithi_number = int(longitude_difference // 12) + 1
    paksha = 'Shukla' if tithi_number <= 15 else 'Krishna'
    tithi_names = ['Pratipada', 'Dwitiya', 'Tritiya', 'Chaturthi', 'Panchami', 'Shashthi', 'Saptami', 'Ashtami', 'Navami', 'Dashami', 'Ekadashi', 'Dwadashi', 'Trayodashi', 'Chaturdashi', 'Purnima', 'Amavasya']
    tithi_index = (tithi_number - 1) % 15
    tithi_name = tithi_names[tithi_index]

    return f"{paksha} {tithi_name}"

This script uses the xlwings library to create an Excel UDF called calculate_tithi that takes a single argument date_input. The rest of the script remains the same.

You can then use this UDF in your Excel sheet like this: =calculate_tithi(A1), where A1 contains the date and time value.

The issue you're facing is due to the way Excel handles user-defined functions (UDFs) and caching.

By default, Excel caches the results of UDFs to improve performance. This means that if the input arguments haven't changed, Excel won't recalculate the UDF.

In your case, the calc_tithi_new function is not being recalculated when you change the date and time in the cell because Excel is using the cached result.

To force Excel to recalculate the UDF dynamically, you can try one of the following:

  1. Volatility: Add the @xw.func(volatile=True) decorator to your calc_tithi_new function. This tells Excel to recalculate the UDF whenever the worksheet changes.
@xw.func(volatile=True)
def calc_tithi_new(date_input):
    # ...
  1. Recalculation: Add a dummy argument to your calc_tithi_new function that changes whenever the date and time change. For example:

12/08/24, 9:23 pm

I understand the issue now. Yes, you are correct. The formula is updating previous cells dynamically because of the way Excel handles UDFs (User-Defined Functions).

When you enter a UDF in a cell, Excel recalculates the entire worksheet, including all cells that contain the UDF. This is because UDFs are volatile, meaning their values can change even if the input arguments don't change.

To avoid this behavior, you can try using the xw.func decorator with the volatile=False argument, like this:

@xw.func(volatile=False)
def calc_tithi_new(date_input):
    # Your function code here

This will tell Excel to treat the UDF as non-volatile, so it will only recalculate the cell when the input arguments change, not when the worksheet is recalculated.

Alternatively, you can also try using the xw.func decorator with the cache=True argument, like this:

@xw.func(cache=True)
def calc_tithi_new(date_input):
    # Your function code here

This will enable caching for the UDF, so Excel will store the results of previous calculations and reuse them instead of recalculating the entire worksheet.

To install Axios in your Windows MSYS2 Node installation, follow these steps:

  1. Open the MSYS2 terminal.
  2. Update the package database by running the command: pacman -Syu
  3. Install Node.js (if you haven't already) using the command: pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-nodejs
  4. Install Axios using npm (Node Package Manager) by running the command: npm install axios
  5. Verify the installation by running the command: npm list axios

If you encounter any issues during the installation process, make sure to check the following:

  • Ensure you are running the MSYS2 terminal as an administrator.
  • Verify that Node.js is installed correctly by running the command: node -v
  • Check for any errors or warnings during the installation process.

After installing Axios, you can import it in your JavaScript files using the following line:

const axios = require('axios');

Note: If you are using a different package manager like yarn, you can install Axios using the command: yarn add axios

Can you explain me about this #define in a C code:
#define GETSEED(rando) asm volatile("1:\n" \
"rdseed %0\n" \
"jnc 1b\n" \
:"=a"(rando) : : "cc")

🤖 Meta AI

14/08/24, 4:29 pm

This #define statement is using the GNU C extension for inline assembly to generate a sequence of assembly instructions. Here's a breakdown of what it does:

  • asm volatile: This tells the compiler to insert the specified assembly code directly into the generated code. The volatile keyword ensures that the compiler doesn't optimize away the assembly code.

  • rdseed %0: This is the assembly instruction to read a random seed from the CPU's random number generator (RDRAND instruction). %0 refers to the first output operand, which is rando in this case.

  • jnc 1b: This is a jump instruction that loops back to label 1 if the carry flag (CF) is not set. The rdseed instruction sets CF if the read was successful.

  • :"=a"(rando): This specifies the output operand for the assembly code. =a means that the operand is written to (modified), and (rando) is the C variable that receives the result.

  • ::: This separates the input and output operands. In this case, there are no input operands.

  • :"cc": This specifies the clobbered registers. In this case, it indicates that the carry flag (CC) is modified by the assembly code.

So, in essence, this #define statement generates assembly code that reads a random seed from the CPU's random number generator and stores it in the variable rando. If the read is unsuccessful, it loops back to try again.

Yes, this C code can be directly written in assembly. Here's the equivalent assembly code using NASM syntax:

asm
section .text
global fill_buf_using_rdseed
global get_bits_using_rdseed

fill_buf_using_rdseed:
    mov     ecx, [rsp + 8]  ; buf_len
    mov     rsi, [rsp + 16] ; buf
    xor     eax, eax
loop_start:
    rdseed  rax
    jc      loop_start
    mov     [rsi], rax
    add     rsi, 8
    loop    loop_start
    ret

get_bits_using_rdseed:
    xor     eax, eax
loop_start:
    rdseed  rax
    jc      loop_start
    ret

Keep in mind that this assembly code is specific to x86-64 architecture and may need modifications for other architectures. Also, the use of rdseed instruction requires a CPU that supports the RDRAND instruction.

  1. Install the nasm package using the command: pacman -S nasm

  2. Create a new file, e.g., random.asm, and paste the assembly code into it.

  3. Assemble the code using the command: nasm -f win64 random.asm -o random.obj

  4. Create a new file, e.g., main.c, and add a simple C program to test the assembly code. For example:

#include <stdio.h>

extern void fill_buf_using_rdseed(uint64_t *buf, uint32_t buf_len);
extern uint64_t get_bits_using_rdseed(void);

int main() {
    uint64_t buf[10];

    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        printf("%llu\n", buf[i]);
    }
    uint64_t random = get_bits_using_rdseed();
    printf("Random number: %llu\n", random);
    return 0;
}

  1. Compile the C program using the command: gcc -c main.c -o main.o

  2. Link the assembled object file with the C program using the command: gcc main.o random.obj -o program.exe

  3. Run the program using the command: ./program.exe

Note: Make sure to use the correct assembler (nasm) and compiler (gcc) flags for 64-bit assembly code. The -f win64 flag tells nasm to generate 64-bit code, and the -c flag tells gcc to compile only, without linking.

  • -no-pie: This option tells GCC not to create a Position Independent Executable (PIE), which is not needed for a simple assembly program.

Note: If you're on a 64-bit system, you might need to use the following command instead:

bash
$ gcc testcode.obj -o testcode.exe -nostdlib -no-pie -m64

The -m64 option tells GCC to generate 64-bit code.

A segmentation fault at runtime can be caused by various issues. Here are some potential causes:

  1. Incorrect memory access: The code might be trying to access memory that is not allocated or is out of bounds.
  2. Null pointer dereference: The code might be trying to access memory through a null pointer.
  3. Stack overflow: The code might be using too much stack space, causing a stack overflow.
  4. Incorrect system call usage: The code might be using system calls incorrectly, causing unexpected behavior.

To troubleshoot the issue, you can try the following:

  1. Use a debugger: Run the program under a debugger like GDB to see where the segmentation fault occurs.

### 🧑 You
*15/08/24, 5:58 pm*

Does following guidance from intel site for rdseed will help you redefine the assembler code:

RDSEED retrieves a hardware-generated random seed value from the SP800-90B and C compliant ENRNG and stores it in the destination register given as an argument to the instruction. Like the RDRAND instruction, the size of the random value is determined by the size of the given register, and the carry flag (CF) must be checked to determine whether or not a random seed was available at the time the instruction was executed.

Also like RDRAND, there are no hardware ring requirements that restrict access to RDSEED based on process privilege level.

To determine programmatically whether a given Intel platform supports the RDSEED instruction, developers can use the CPUID instruction to examine bit 18 of the EBX register. See Reference (8) for details.

### 🤖 Meta AI
*15/08/24, 5:58 pm*

Yes, following the guidance from the Intel site for RDSEED can help redefine the assembler code.

Based on the Intel documentation, here's an updated version of the assembler code that uses RDSEED correctly:

asm
section .text
extern printf
global _start

_start:
; Check if RDSEED is supported
mov eax, 1
cpuid
test ebx, 1<<18
jz unsupported

; Generate a random seed using RDSEED
rdseed rax
jc try_again

; Check if a random seed was available
jnc seed_available

try_again:
jmp _start

seed_available:
; Print the random seed using printf
mov rdi, format
mov rsi, rax
xor eax, eax
call printf

; Exit the program
mov eax, 60
xor edi, edi
syscall

unsupported:
; Exit the program with an error code if RDSEED is unsupported
mov eax, 60
mov edi, 1
syscall

section .data
format: db '%llu', 0xA, 0

This updated code:

1. Checks if RDSEED is supported using CPUID.
2. Generates a random seed using RDSEED.
3. Checks if a random seed was available by examining the carry flag (CF).
4. If a seed is available, prints it using printf.
5. Exits the program.

Note that I've removed the `debug_msg` and `try_again` label, as they're no longer needed. Also, I've added a `seed_available` label to handle the case where a random seed is available.

rdrand rax
jc low_entropy

; Generate a random seed using rdseed

rdseed_loop:
rdseed eax
jc rdseed_loop

; Print the value of EAX after RDSEED
mov rsi, rax
mov rax, 1
mov rdi, 1
mov rdx, 8
syscall

; Print a message indicating whether RDSEED was successful
mov rax, 1
mov rdi, 1
mov rsi, successful_msg
mov rdx, 12
syscall
jmp next_trial

print_not_successful:
mov rax, 1
mov rdi, 1
mov rsi, not_successful_msg
mov rdx, 15
syscall

rdseed_failed:
; Print a message indicating that RDSEED failed
mov rax, 1
mov rdi, 1
mov rsi, rdseed_failed_msg
mov rdx, 15
syscall

low_entropy:
; Print a message indicating low entropy
mov rax, 1
mov rdi, 1
mov rsi, low_entropy_msg
mov rdx, 13
syscall

next_trial:
; Decrement trial count
dec dword [trial_count]
mov ecx, [trial_count]
cmp ecx, 0
jg trial_loop

; Exit if all trials failed
mov rax, 60
mov rdi, 1
syscall

seed_available:
; Exit the program
mov rax, 60
xor rdi, rdi
syscall

unsupported:
; Exit the program with an error code if RDSEED is unsupported
mov rax, 60
mov rdi, 1
syscall

section .data
successful_msg: db "Successful", 0xA
not_successful_msg: db "Not successful", 0xA
rdseed_failed_msg: db "RDSEED failed", 0xA
low_entropy_msg: db "Low entropy", 0xA
trial_count: dd 0

This code will print the 64-bit random number generated by `rdseed` if it succeeds, or an error message if it fails.

*17/08/24, 1:16 pm*

The error message indicates that there's a relocation truncated to fit issue. This usually occurs when the linker tries to fit a 64-bit address into a 32-bit field.

In your case, the issue is likely due to the fact that you're using the `rdseed` instruction, which generates a 64-bit random number, but the `mov [rand64], rax` instruction is trying to store it in a 32-bit memory location.

To fix this, you need to change the `rand64` variable to a 64-bit memory location. You can do this by changing the `resq 1` directive to `resq 2` in the `.bss` section:

asm
section .bss
rand64: resq 2

This will allocate 16 bytes (2 quadwords) for the `rand64` variable, which should be enough to store the 64-bit random number generated by `rdseed`.

Additionally, you may need to adjust the code that uses the `rand64` variable to account for the changed memory layout.

After making these changes, try reassembling and linking the code to see if the issue is resolved.

The code you provided is for Linux, and it uses system calls specific to Linux. To compile and run this code on Windows, you'll need to make some modifications.

Here are the main differences:

1. System calls: Windows uses a different set of system calls than Linux. You'll need to replace the Linux system calls with their Windows equivalents.

2. Linking: The linker command is different for Windows. You'll need to use a linker that supports Windows executables, such as `ld` with the `--subsystem=console` option or `go-link`.

3. Assembly format: The assembly format is different for Windows. You'll need to use the `win64` format instead of `elf64`.

Here's an example of how you can modify your code to compile and run on Windows:

asm
section .text
global _start

_start:
; Generate a 64-bit random number using rdseed
rdseed rax
mov qword [rand64], rax

; Convert the 64-bit random number to a hexadecimal string
lea rsi, [rand64]
call hex_to_str

; Print the hexadecimal string
mov rax, 1
mov rdi, 1
mov rsi, hex_buffer
mov rdx, 17
syscall

; ... (rest of the code remains the same)

section .bss
rand64: resq 1
hex_buffer: resb 17
dec_buffer: resb 21

section .data
newline: db 0xa

To compile and link this code on Windows, use the following commands:

bash
nasm -f win64 test.asm -o test.o
ld --subsystem=console -o test.exe test.o

Or, you can use `go-link` instead of `ld`:

bash
go-link -o test.exe test.o

Note that this code still uses Linux-style system calls, which won't work on Windows. You'll need to replace these with Windows-specific system calls or use a library that provides a compatible interface.

### 🤖 Meta AI
*18/08/24, 5:14 pm*

You are correct, I previously mentioned that on Windows, `rsi` is not used as the source index register, but instead, the `lea` instruction is used to load the address of the buffer into the `rdx` register.

However, in the context of the `hex_to_dec` function, `rsi` is being used as the input parameter register, not as the source index register. This is a common convention in Windows x64 calling convention, where `rsi` is used to pass the first parameter to a function.

So, in the code snippet you mentioned, `rsi` is being used correctly to pass the address of `rand64` to the `hex_to_dec` function.

Thank you for pointing out the potential confusion!

import xlwings as xw
import pandas as pd
from ta.trend import wma_indicator

@xw.func
def weaverage(close, window, fillna=False):
"""Calculate the Weighted Moving Average (WMA) for the given close prices.

Parameters:
    close (list of lists): Input range from Excel.
    window (int): Window size for WMA calculation.
    fillna (bool): Fill NaN values with False.

Returns:
    list: Weighted Moving Average (WMA) series.
"""
# Convert the list of lists to a pandas Series
close_series = pd.Series(close[0])

# Calculate the WMA
wma = wma_indicator(close_series, window=window, fillna=fillna)

# Return the WMA as a list
return wma.tolist()

This UDF expects the input range `close` to be a list of lists, where the inner list contains the close prices. The `window` parameter is an integer, and the `fillna` parameter is a boolean (defaulting to `False`).

The UDF converts the input range to a pandas Series, calculates the WMA using the `ta` library, and returns the result as a list.

You can then use this UDF in Excel by calling it with the appropriate inputs, like this:

`=weaverage(A1:A10, 9, FALSE)`

Replace `A1:A10` with the actual range of close prices, and adjust the window size and fillna flag as needed.

### 🤖 Meta AI
*21/08/24, 5:49 pm*

Here are the steps to install Visual Studio without admin rights on Windows:

*Step 1: Download the Visual Studio Installer*

- Go to the Visual Studio download page and click on the "Download" button for the version you want to install (e.g., Visual Studio 2022).
- Save the installer file (e.g., `vs_Enterprise.exe`) to a location on your machine.

*Step 2: Run the Installer and Update*

- Run the installer file (e.g., `vs_Enterprise.exe`) as a standard user (non-admin).
- Follow the prompts to update the installer. This will download and install the latest version of the installer.
- Once the update is complete, cancel the setup process. This will exit the installer.

*Step 3: Set the Global Policy*

- Open the Registry Editor (Regedit.exe) as a standard user (non-admin).
- Navigate to the following key: `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\VisualStudio\Setup`
- Create a new DWORD (32-bit) value named `AllowStandardUserControl` and set its value to `2`.
- Close the Registry Editor.

*Step 4: Run the Installer Again*

- Run the installer file (e.g., `vs_Enterprise.exe`) again as a standard user (non-admin).
- This time, you should be able to install Visual Studio without admin rights.

Note: The `AllowStandardUserControl` policy allows standard users to perform installer actions, including modify and install, from the Available tab.

Please be aware that these steps are based on the guidance you provided and might not work in all scenarios. Additionally, installing software without admin rights may have limitations and risks, so proceed with caution.

MASM uses the `.model` directive to specify the memory model, and the `.386` or `.686` directive to specify the processor architecture.

Here's the corrected code:

.model flat, stdcall
option casemap :none

extrn WriteConsoleA: PROC
extrn ExitProcess: PROC

STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE equ -11

.data
rand64 QWORD 0

dec_buffer BYTE 21 DUP(0)
newline BYTE 0Ah, 0

.data?
stdout_handle QWORD ?

; ... (rest of the code remains the same)

myVar MY128BIT <>

The errors you're seeing are due to the fact that the instructions and data are not properly segmented in your assembly code.

In MASM (Microsoft Macro Assembler) syntax, which UASM (Ulf Assembler) is compatible with, code and data need to be enclosed in segments. The `.DATA` segment is used for initialized data, and the `.CODE` segment is used for code.

Here's the corrected code:

extrn printf: PROC

.DATA
rand64 QWORD 0
hex_buffer BYTE 17 DUP(0) ; 16 bytes + null terminator
dec_buffer BYTE 21 DUP(0) ; 20 bytes + null terminator
newline BYTE 0Ah, 0

.CODE
main PROC
; Set CPU to x64 mode for 64-bit instructions
USE64

; Generate a 64-bit random number using rdseed
rdseed rax
mov [rand64], rax

; Convert the 64-bit random number to a hexadecimal string
lea rsi, [rand64]
call hex_to_str

; Print the hexadecimal string
lea rcx, [hex_buffer]
call printf_internal

; Print a newline after the hexadecimal number
lea rcx, [newline]
call printf_internal

; Convert hexadecimal to decimal
lea rsi, [rand64]
call hex_to_dec

; Print the decimal value
lea rcx, [dec_buffer]
call printf_internal

; Print a newline after the decimal number
lea rcx, [newline]
call printf_internal

; Exit the program
ret

main ENDP

hex_to_str PROC
; Convert the 64-bit number in rsi to a hexadecimal string in hex_buffer
mov rax, [rsi]
lea rdi, [hex_buffer + 15]
mov rcx, 16
mov rbx, 16
mov byte ptr [rdi + 1], 0 ; Null-terminate the string
convert_hex_loop:
xor rdx, rdx
div rbx
add dl, '0'
cmp dl, '9'
jbe store_hex
add dl, 7
store_hex:
mov [rdi], dl
dec rdi
loop convert_hex_loop
ret
hex_to_str ENDP

hex_to_dec PROC
; Convert the 64-bit number in rsi to a decimal string in dec_buffer
mov rax, [rsi]
lea rdi, [dec_buffer + 20] ; Point to the end of the buffer (before null terminator)
mov rcx, 20 ; Maximum digits for a 64-bit number in decimal
mov rbx, 10 ; Base 10 for decimal conversion
mov byte ptr [rdi], 0 ; Null-terminate the string
dec rdi
convert_dec_loop:
xor rdx, rdx ; Clear rdx before division
div rbx ; Divide rax by 10, rdx will have remainder
add dl, '0' ; Convert remainder to ASCII
mov [rdi], dl ; Store the digit
dec rdi ; Move to the previous byte
dec rcx ; Decrease digit count
test rax, rax ; Check if rax is zero
jnz convert_dec_loop ; If not, continue loop
; Now rdi points to the position just before the first digit.
; If rcx > 0, we need to pad with leading zeros.
mov al, '0' ; ASCII for '0'
pad_zeroes:
cmp rcx, 0 ; Check if padding is needed
jz finish_padding ; If no more padding needed, exit loop
mov [rdi], al ; Pad with '0'
dec rdi ; Move to the previous byte
dec rcx ; Decrease digit count
jmp pad_zeroes ; Repeat until fully padded
finish_padding:
lea rdi, [rdi + 1] ; Adjust rdi to point to the first digit
ret
hex_to_dec ENDP

printf_internal PROC
sub rsp, 20h ; Allocate stack space for alignment
call printf ; Call printf from msvcrt.lib
add rsp, 20h ; Clean up stack space
ret
printf_internal ENDP

END main

Note that I've also added `END main` at the end of the code to specify the entry point of the program.

### 🤖 Meta AI
*31/08/24, 9:58 am*

The Excel Java API does not provide an add-in like interface similar to xlwings. However, you can create a Java-based Excel add-in using the Excel Java API and the IDTExtensibility2 interface. Here's a step-wise process to access a Java UDF from Excel:

1. _Create a Java project_: Set up a Java project in your preferred IDE (e.g., Eclipse, IntelliJ).

2. _Add dependencies_: Include the Excel Java API and the IDTExtensibility2 interface in your project.

3. _Implement the IDTExtensibility2 interface_: Create a Java class that implements the IDTExtensibility2 interface. This will allow your add-in to interact with Excel.

4. _Register the add-in_: Register your add-in with Excel using the IDTExtensibility2 interface.

5. _Create a UDF_: Write a Java method that will serve as your UDF.

6. _Expose the UDF to Excel_: Use the Excel Java API to expose your UDF to Excel.

7. _Build and deploy the add-in_: Build your Java project and deploy the add-in to Excel.

8. _Access the UDF from Excel_: Once the add-in is deployed, you can access your Java UDF from Excel using the `=` operator, just like a built-in Excel function.

Here's a simple example to get you started:

import com.microsoft.office.interop.excel.IDTExtensibility2;
import com.microsoft.office.interop.excel.XlUDF;

public class MyAddIn implements IDTExtensibility2 {
@Override
public void onConnection(Object application, Object connectMode, Object addInInst, Object custom) {
// Register the UDF with Excel
XlUDF udf = new XlUDF();
udf.setName("MyJavaUDF");
udf.setFunction(new MyJavaUDF());
application.getUDFs().add(udf);
}
}

public class MyJavaUDF implements com.microsoft.office.interop.excel.XlUDF {
@Override
public String evaluate(String[] args) {
// Your UDF logic here
return "Hello from Java!";
}
}

Note that this is a simplified example and may require additional steps and configuration to work in your environment.

Let's achieve something more useful. Modify the example code to get input in UDF as excel range and output as string converted from numbers in the array. If input is not a number - you have include that check or an exception - then return "" (null). Output shall obviously be an array.

### 🤖 Meta AI
*31/08/24, 10:06 am*

Here's the modified Java code for the UDF:

import com.microsoft.office.interop.excel.XlUDF;
import com.microsoft.office.interop.excel.XlArray;
import com.microsoft.office.interop.excel.XlRange;

public class MyJavaUDF implements XlUDF {
@Override
public String[] evaluate(XlArray xlArray) {
String[] result = new String[xlArray.getRowDimension()];
for (int i = 1; i <= xlArray.getRowDimension(); i++) {
for (int j = 1; j <= xlArray.getColumnDimension(); j++) {
Object value = xlArray.getValue(i, j);
if (value instanceof Double) {
result[i - 1] += String.valueOf(value);
} else {
result[i - 1] += "";
}
}
}
return result;
}
}

And here's the modified `MyAddIn` class to register the UDF:

import com.microsoft.office.interop.excel.IDTExtensibility2;
import com.microsoft.office.interop.excel.XlUDF;

public class MyAddIn implements IDTExtensibility2 {
@Override
public void onConnection(Object application, Object connectMode, Object addInInst, Object custom) {
// Register the UDF with Excel
XlUDF udf = new XlUDF();
udf.setName("MyJavaUDF");
udf.setFunction(new MyJavaUDF());
udf.setArgTypes(new int[]{XlUDF.XlArgType.xlRange});
udf.setReturnType(XlUDF.XlReturnType.xlString);
application.getUDFs().add(udf);
}
}

In this modified code:

- The `evaluate` method takes an `XlArray` as input, representing the Excel range.
- It iterates over the array, checks if each value is a number (instance of `Double`), and converts it to a string if it is.
- If the value is not a number, it returns an empty string.
- The method returns an array of strings.

Note that I've also updated the `MyAddIn` class to specify the input argument type as `xlRange` and the return type as `xlString`.

With this modified code, you can use the UDF in Excel like this:

`=MyJavaUDF(A1:B2)`

Assuming the range `A1:B2` contains numbers, the UDF will return an array of strings representing those numbers. If the range contains non-numeric values, they will be replaced with empty strings in the output array.

To compile your files into an `.xll` add-in using MSYS2 and GCC/G++, follow these steps:

1. Open the MSYS2 terminal and navigate to the folder containing your files.

2. Compile each `.cpp` file into an object file using the following commands:

bash
g++ -c BinaryProtocol.cpp -o BinaryProtocol.o
g++ -c SheetGenerator.cpp -o SheetGenerator.o

g++ -c JSONCodec.cpp -o JSONCodec.o
g++ -c XLCodec.cpp -o XLCodec.o

bash
g++ -shared -o xlloop.dll BinaryProtocol.o SheetGenerator.o XLUtil.o HttpProtocol.o JSONCodec.o XLCodec.o Timeout.o -Wl,--out-implib,libxlloop.a

LIBRARY xlloop
EXPORTS
xlAutoOpen @1

xlAddInManagerInfo @3
xlUDFTest @4

bash

1. Compile the `xlcall.cpp` file into an object file:

g++ -c xlcall.cpp -o xlcall.o

1. Link the `xlcall.o` object file with the `libxlloop.a` import library to create the final `.xll` add-in:

bash

### 🤖 Meta AI
*01/09/24, 1:38 pm*

The issue you're encountering is due to the way Excel handles regular expressions, particularly when using the `.*` wildcard. When Excel encounters a pattern ending with `.*$`, it expects the entire cell value to match the pattern, including the newline character at the end. Since the newline character is not present in the cell value, Excel returns a `#CALC!` error.

To resolve this issue, you can modify the regular expression to make the `.*` wildcard lazy by adding a `?` after it, like this: `.*?$`. This will make the wildcard match as few characters as possible, including none, allowing the pattern to match the entire cell value without expecting a newline character.

Alternatively, you can remove the `$` anchor from the pattern, like this: `.*?`. This will allow the pattern to match any characters in the cell value, without expecting a newline character at the end.

Here's the updated function with the modified regular expression:

import re

@xw.func
@xw.arg('excel_range', ndim=2)
@xw.arg('patterns', ndim=1)
def REGEXFINDM(excel_range, patterns):
result = []
for row in excel_range:
row_result = []
for cell in row:
cell_str = str(cell) # Convert cell to string
cell_result = []
for pattern in patterns:
match = re.search(pattern + '.*?', cell_str, flags=re.UNICODE)
if match:
cell_result.append(cell_str) # Return the entire string
if len(cell_result) == len(patterns):
row_result.append(" ".join(cell_result))
else:
row_result.append("")
result.append(row_result)
return result

Note that I added `+ '.*?'` to the `pattern` variable in the `re.search` function. This will make the pattern match any characters in the cell value, without expecting a newline character at the end.

*03/02/25, 9:36 pm*

Here's an optimized version of the code:

import xlwings as xw
import numpy as np

@xw.func
def Offset_Value(input_range, value_threshold, offset_row, offset_column):
# Convert input_range to a NumPy array
input_array = np.array(input_range)

# Calculate total rows and columns
total_rows, total_cols = input_array.shape

# Initialize results array with empty strings
results = np.full((total_rows, total_cols), "", dtype=object)

# Process matches and store at correct positions
for i, j in zip(*np.where(input_array == value_threshold)):
    offset_i, offset_j = i + offset_row, j + offset_column
    if (0 <= offset_i < total_rows) and (0 <= offset_j < total_cols):
        results[i, j] = input_array[offset_i, offset_j]
    else:
        results[i, j] = "Offset out of range"

return results.tolist()

2. *Vectorized operations*: Used NumPy's vectorized operations (`np.where`, `np.full`) to reduce the need for explicit loops.

4. *Removed unnecessary variables*: Removed variables like `input_list`, `total_cells`, and `pos` that were not necessary for the computation.

These changes should result in significant performance improvements, especially for large input ranges.

In current times between gcc and clang / llvm, which eco system is the backbone of all AI LLM?

🤖 Meta AI

10/05/26, 12:56 pm

Neither GCC nor Clang/LLVM is "the backbone" by itself, but LLVM/Clang is the dominant ecosystem for AI/LLM development today.

Why LLVM/Clang leads for AI/LLMs:

  1. Compiler infrastructure for accelerators
    NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, Intel oneAPI, Google TPU XLA, and Apple Metal all use LLVM as the backend. When you train Llama, GPT, Claude, Gemini - the kernels running on GPU/TPU are compiled through LLVM-based toolchains.
  2. MLIR = LLVM's ML dialect
    MLIR "Multi-Level IR" was created inside LLVM specifically for ML compilers. It's now the backbone of:
  3. TensorFlow XLA
  4. PyTorch torch.compile + Triton
  5. JAX
  6. OpenAI Triton DSL
  7. Mojo language
    GCC has no equivalent ML compiler infrastructure.
  8. JIT + cross-compilation
    LLMs need to fuse kernels at runtime and target NVIDIA/AMD/Intel/ARM/TPU. LLVM was designed for JIT and retargetable backends. GCC is primarily ahead-of-time for CPU.
  9. Major frameworks
  10. PyTorch: Triton -> LLVM, torch.compile -> Inductor -> LLVM
  11. JAX: XLA -> MLIR -> LLVM
  12. TensorFlow: XLA -> MLIR -> LLVM
  13. vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, http://llama.cpp: All built with Clang by default for perf + CUDA/HIP interop

Where GCC is still used:
GCC is still the default for building CPython, many Linux distros, and some legacy HPC code. But for the actual LLM runtime kernels, GCC is rarely touched.

Bottom line:
If you delete LLVM tomorrow, CUDA, ROCm, PyTorch, JAX, Triton, and 90% of LLM inference engines break. If you delete GCC, most LLM stacks keep running fine because they already build with Clang.

So for current LLM work: LLVM/Clang ecosystem wins. GCC is still critical for Linux/CPU, but not the backbone of AI.

10/05/26, 1:00 pm

In spite of these hard facts why no linux distros and even kernel not making attempt to port to llvm / clang where the future is? In fact if they port, integration with LLM will be a bliss for them

🤖 Meta AI

10/05/26, 1:00 pm

Short answer: inertia, GCC extensions, and "it works" beats "the future" until there's a forcing function.

Why Linux + most distros still stick with GCC

  1. GCC extensions in kernel code
    The Linux kernel uses a ton of GCC-specific extensions: asm goto, nested functions, variable-length arrays in structs, *attribute*((cleanup)), statement expressions. Many were non-standard C. LLVM/Clang had to implement most of them just to compile the kernel. Up to ∼2021 you literally couldn't boot mainline Linux built with Clang.

  2. Distro-wide rebuild risk
    A distro = 30k+ packages. Switching compiler means you re-test everything. GCC has decades of bug-compatibility baked into userspace. Change compiler, you get new miscompiles, new UB explosions, new ABI edge cases. Debian tried Clang rebuilds: thousands of packages FTBFS. Maintainers don't have time to patch every project just because LLVM is "the future".

  3. Performance parity is recent
    For x86_64 kernel code, GCC often still wins by 1-3% on throughput. Kernel devs are obsessed with perf regressions. Until ∼2019 Clang was slower on kernel workloads. "Blissful LLM integration" doesn't pay the cost of losing 2% syscall throughput on every server.

  4. Tooling ecosystem
    GCC plugins, kernel sanitizers, kpatch, LTO, PGO workflows were GCC-first. Clang caught up, but distros standardize on one toolchain to avoid maintaining 2x CI, 2x bug triage, 2x security audits.

Where Clang is happening

  1. Linux kernel officially supports Clang since 5.15. Google builds Android kernels + ChromeOS kernels with Clang. Meta and Amazon use Clang for internal kernels. CC=clang works today.
  2. Distros: Alpine, Chimera Linux, Android, OpenMandriva build major parts with Clang. FreeBSD ditched GCC years ago and is fully LLVM.
  3. Google's plan: They want Clang everywhere for LTO/CFI/randstruct to harden Android. That's driving upstream kernel Clang support.

Why "LLM integration bliss" isn't a driver

Kernel/distro maintainers don't care about LLMs. Their job: boot fast, don't crash, don't regress, pass security audits. An LLM-friendly compiler gives them zero benefit. The people who need LLVM for AI already use it: PyTorch, CUDA, Triton all ship their own LLVM toolchains independent of /usr/bin/cc.

The integration point isn't the distro compiler. It's that your Python wheels ship pre-compiled LLVM-IR or PTX. Whether Ubuntu was built with GCC or Clang doesn't affect pip install torch.

So will they port?
Gradually, yes. But not for AI hype. They'll switch when Clang gives better security hardening, better diagnostics, faster builds, or when GCC stops maintaining an arch. "Future is LLVM" isn't enough to break 30 years of working code.

Want the real bliss? Build userspace with Clang/LLVM while kernel stays GCC. Many already do that. Distros are pragmatic, not ideological.

Python is also all gcc under the hood?

🤖 Meta AI

10/05/26, 1:06 pm

No, CPython is not "all GCC under the hood". It depends on what platform and who built it.

CPython source is portable C
The reference Python interpreter is written in standard C89/C11 with POSIX extensions. It has no hard dependency on GCC. The build system uses whatever cc you give it.

What actually builds Python today:
Platform / Distro Compiler used
http://python.org Windows builds MSVC
macOS + Homebrew Apple Clang
Ubuntu/Debian/Fedora official python3 GCC
Alpine Linux GCC or Clang, varies
Android Termux Clang
Conda-Forge Python GCC on Linux, Clang on macOS, MSVC on Win
Google internal Python Clang
Meta/Facebook Python Clang
So GCC is common on Linux distros, but not universal.

The extension modules = different story
The parts that matter for AI/LLM are not "Python". They are C/C++/CUDA extensions:

  1. NumPy: GCC or Clang, but SIMD kernels often use Clang for better autovec
  2. PyTorch: 100% Clang + NVCC. torch.compile uses LLVM/MLIR/Triton
  3. JAX/XLA: Clang + MLIR + LLVM
  4. llama.cpp: Clang preferred, GCC works but slower
  5. CUDA kernels: NVCC uses an LLVM fork under the hood

So while your /usr/bin/python3 might be GCC-built, the moment you import torch, you're running code compiled by LLVM/Clang/Triton.

Why people think "Python = GCC"
1. python3-config --cflags on Ubuntu spits out -D_GNU_SOURCE. That's from GCC.
2. pip install from source invokes gcc by default on Linux because distros set CC=gcc.
3. The manylinux wheels are built with GCC for glibc compatibility.

But none of that is fundamental. CPython builds fine with Clang: CC=clang ./configure && make. Many people do it for PGO + LTO because Clang often gives 5-10% faster Python.

Bottom line
CPython core: compiler-agnostic, but distros pick GCC for legacy reasons.
AI/LLM Python ecosystem: overwhelmingly LLVM/Clang/Triton.

So "Python is all GCC" was true in 2010. In 2026, the Python you use for LLMs is mostly Clang/LLVM the second you leave the stdlib.

So python has many code sources - gcc, clang, msvc, etc. compatible?

🤖 Meta AI

10/05/26, 1:08 pm

Yep. CPython core is written to be compiler-agnostic, not tied to GCC.

The source is portable C
CPython targets C11 + POSIX. No GCC builtins required. It avoids *attribute* unless wrapped in #ifdef *GNUC*. Same for MSVC __declspec and Clang specifics. The configure script + pyconfig.h detect features at build time.

So the exact same .c files compile with:
- GCC on Linux/BSD
- Clang on macOS, Android, FreeBSD, and increasingly Linux
- MSVC on Windows
- Intel ICC/ICX, IBM XL C, even TinyCC if you're stubborn

What makes it work across compilers

  1. Conditional compilation
    #if defined(GNUC)
    #define Py_GCC_ATTRIBUTE(x) attribute(x)
    #else
    #define Py_GCC_ATTRIBUTE(x)
    #endif
    Same pattern for MSVC, Clang. Features degrade gracefully.

  2. PEP 7 C style
    Strict subset of C that all major compilers understand. No VLA, no nested functions, no statement expressions in core code.

  3. Build system abstraction
    setup.py and Makefile query distutils.sysconfig to get flags from the compiler that built Python. So extensions use the same compiler by default, keeping ABI sane.

The catch: extensions and ABI
Compiler compatibility ≠ ABI compatibility.
OS Rule
Linux GCC and Clang are mostly ABI-compatible for C. So a GCC Python can load a Clang-built .so. C++ extensions are riskier due to libstdc++ vs libc++.
Windows MSVC version must match. Python 3.11 = MSVC 193x. GCC-mingw wheels won't load into http://python.org Python.
macOS Apple Clang is the system ABI. GCC from homebrew works too since it's really Clang.
This is why wheels exist. manylinux2014_x86_64 assumes GCC + glibc. If you build extensions with Clang you test them hard before shipping.

AI/LLM angle
The core interpreter compiler barely matters for LLM speed. 99% of runtime is in extensions: PyTorch, NumPy, Triton, CUDA. Those are overwhelmingly Clang/LLVM regardless of how Python itself was built.

So yes: CPython source is multi-compiler compatible by design. But your running Python process in 2026 is usually a mix - maybe GCC-built interpreter, loading Clang-built NumPy, JITing Triton kernels via LLVM. The compilers play nice at the C ABI layer.

Want max speed? Build CPython itself with CC=clang + PGO + LTO. It's officially supported since 3.6 and often 10% faster than distro GCC builds.

Exactly. One C codebase, but it "shapeshifts" at compile time based on the platform + compiler.

Think of it like this:

1. Same .c files for everyone
There's only one Objects/longobject.c, one Python/ceval.c. No separate GCC version vs MSVC version in the repo.

2. #ifdef fences everywhere
The code is littered with conditional blocks that activate depending on what the build system detects:

ifdef _WIN32

/* Windows-specific code using MSVC APIs */

elif defined(APPLE)

/* macOS specific, assumes Clang */

elif defined(linux)

/* Linux code, works with GCC or Clang */

endif

if defined(GNUC) && !defined(clang)

/* GCC-only builtin */

elif defined(clang)

/* Clang-only builtin */

elif defined(_MSC_VER)

/* MSVC-only pragma */

endif

3. configure + pyconfig.h do the detective work
When you run ./configure, it probes the compiler:
1. "Do you have <unistd.h>?" -> #define HAVE_UNISTD_H 1
2. "Does *attribute*((visibility)) work?" -> #define HAVE_GCC_ASM_FOR_X87 1
3. "What's the size of long?" -> #define SIZEOF_LONG 8

All results dump into pyconfig.h. Then the C code includes that and compiles different paths.

4. Distutils/setuptools inherit the choice
Once Python itself is built with GCC, python3-config --cflags tells all extensions "hey, use these same GCC flags". So pip-compile also uses GCC by default. Build with Clang, extensions default to Clang. Keeps the ABI consistent.

So it's not "runtime detection"
The decision is baked in at compile time. A http://python.org Windows python.exe has the MSVC branches compiled in, and the GCC/Clang branches are completely gone from the binary. Your Ubuntu /usr/bin/python3 has the GCC/Linux branches, no MSVC code.

Why this matters for you
You can take the exact CPython 3.13 tarball and build it 3 times:
Command Result
CC=gcc ./configure && make GCC-optimized binary, GNU extensions used
CC=clang ./configure && make Clang-optimized, LTO/PGO friendly, often faster
cl on Windows MSVC binary, .pyd extensions only
Same source, 3 different binaries, all legit Python.

So yeah: one C codebase, but heavy use of preprocessor conditionals + configure tests to morph into the right shape for each compiler/OS. That's how it stays portable without forking the code.

Where the extra effort shows up:

  1. Writing the conditionals
    Someone had to figure out "GCC has *builtin_expect, MSVC has *assume, Clang has both". Then wrap it:
    #if defined(GNUC) || defined(clang)
    #define Py_UNLIKELY(x) __builtin_expect((x), 0)
    #elif defined(_MSC_VER)
    #define Py_UNLIKELY(x) (x)
    #else
    #define Py_UNLIKELY(x) (x)
    #endif
    Multiply that by 200+ feature checks. That's real engineering time.

  2. Testing matrix explodes
    You can't just test on Ubuntu + GCC. CI has to build with: GCC, Clang, MSVC, 32-bit, 64-bit, musl, glibc, big-endian, Windows, macOS. One #ifdef *linux* can hide a bug that only hits FreeBSD. CPython's buildbot fleet exists because of this.

  3. Maintenance debt
    Each branch can rot. Example: Python used to have #ifdef __TANDEM for NonStop OS. Nobody touched it for 10 years, then it broke the build. Someone had to either fix it or delete it. The "price" of portability is deleting dead platforms constantly.

  4. Performance footguns
    You write fast path for GCC intrinsics, slow fallback for other compilers. Now Clang users get the slow path unless someone adds Clang-specific code too. So you either duplicate effort or accept regressions.

  5. Readability hit
    Code like this is common in CPython:
    #if defined(MS_WINDOWS)
    / 20 lines of WinAPI /
    #elif defined(wasi)
    / 5 lines for WASM /
    #else
    / POSIX /
    #endif
    New contributors have to mentally compile the preprocessor to understand control flow.

Why they still do it
Alternative is worse: fork the codebase per compiler/OS. That’s what OpenSSL tried pre-1.1 and it was a nightmare. One tree + conditionals keeps patches, security fixes, and features in sync.

Also, most of the cost is front-loaded. Once pyport.h abstracts Py_ssize_t or Py_FORCEINLINE, the rest of the code just uses the macro and forgets about compilers.

The LLM angle
This is exactly why LLVM/MLIR is winning for AI. Instead of #ifdef NVCC vs #ifdef HIP vs #ifdef METAL, you write one MLIR dialect and let LLVM backends handle it. CPython predates that luxury. It pays the #ifdef tax so you don't have to.

So yeah: portability = extra code, extra tests, extra bugs. CPython eats that cost so import sys works the same on your laptop and on a supercomputer.

1. Go

syscall_windows.go //go:build windows
syscall_linux.go //go:build linux
syscall_darwin.go //go:build darwin
Same function name in each file. go build picks one. So the "extra effort" is still there, but it's cleaner than C macros. You only write OS code if you touch files, network, time. Pure Go code is 100% portable.

2. Rust
Rust is LLVM-only, so compiler differences vanish. But OS differences stay:

[cfg(target_os = "windows")]

fn get_pid() -> u32 { / WinAPI / }

[cfg(unix)]

fn get_pid() -> u32 { / libc / }
The Rust stdlib eats most of this cost. std::fs::File works everywhere because std wrote the cfg blocks. You only drop to #[cfg] when doing FFI or raw syscalls. So less pain than C, but not zero.

3. Java
Your .class files have zero conditionals. File f = new File("foo") compiles once. The OpenJDK source has the #ifdef _WIN32 hell inside the JVM C++ code. So the language designers paid the tax so app devs don't. Tradeoff: JVM startup cost + harder FFI.

4. http://Node.js / JavaScript
JS itself is OS-agnostic. All the pain is in libuv, the C library Node uses for async I/O. libuv has a ton of #ifdef _WIN32 to emulate epoll with IOCP. You never see it. fs.readFile just works. But Node core devs definitely feel the same C portability tax as CPython.

5. Ada
GNAT compiler + runtime does the abstraction. Ada spec says package Calendar works everywhere. The GNAT runtime has target-specific bodies. So again, language implementers eat the cost, users don't.

The LLVM twist for Rust
You said "Rust is essentially clang/llvm". True for codegen, but OS ABI still differs. Windows SEH vs Unix DWARF exceptions, msvc vs gnu target, struct layout, calling convention. So Rust still has #[cfg(target_env = "msvc")] in std. LLVM removes compiler differences, not OS differences.

Bottom line
Every language hits POSIX vs Win32 vs macOS eventually. The question is: do you write the #ifdef, or does the stdlib/runtime do it for you?

C/Python: you often do.
Go/Rust: stdlib does 95%, you do 5%.
Java/JS: runtime does 99.9%, you do 0.1%.

The "extra coding effort" never disappears. It just gets pushed down the stack to whoever ships the runtime. For AI/LLM code, that's why people like Python + PyTorch: the PyTorch team ate the CUDA/ROCm/Metal #ifdef pain so you can write x.to('cuda') once.

🤖 Meta AI

25/06/26, 6:06 pm

That code is already pretty solid — you caught the main ones. But there are still real bugs and gotchas left.

1. Compile-time guard is wrong for MSVC

if !defined(RDSEED) && !defined(_MSC_VER)

#error "Compile with -mrdseed flag to enable RDSEED support"

endif

MSVC doesn't define *RDSEED* and doesn't use -mrdseed. _rdseed64_step exists as long as you're on VS2015+ targeting x64. This guard will incorrectly force an error on MSVC. Should be:

if !defined(RDSEED) && !defined(clang) && !defined(_MSC_VER)

Or better: drop the guard entirely. You already do runtime CPUID check, so compiling without -mrdseed just makes _rdseed64_step unresolved. Let the linker tell you.

2. unsigned long long ≠ always 8 bytes
You assume sizeof(unsigned long long) == 8 for memcpy(buf + i * 8, &val, 8). True on x86_64 Linux/Windows, but the C standard only guarantees >= 64 bits. Use uint64_t from <stdint.h> instead:
uint64_t val;
if (_rdseed64_step(&val)) {
memcpy(buf + i * 8, &val, sizeof(uint64_t));
And validate n_bytes % sizeof(uint64_t) != 0 instead of hardcoding 8.

3. _rdseed64_step not available on 32-bit
On 32-bit x86 there's only _rdseed32_step. Your code will fail to compile for i386 builds of Python. Guard it:

if defined(x86_64) || defined(_M_X64)

uint64_t val;
if (_rdseed64_step(&val)) { ... }

else

unsigned int val;
if (_rdseed32_step(&val)) { ... memcpy(..., 4); }

endif

And then n_bytes must be multiple of 4 on 32-bit. Otherwise reject or handle mixed.

4. py_has_rdseed ignores Python args but signature is wrong
You declared py_has_rdseed as METH_NOARGS, but function signature is (PyObject _self, PyObject _args). For METH_NOARGS it must be (PyObject _self, PyObject _Py_UNUSED(ignored)). GCC will warn, and some compilers will miscompile. Fix:
static PyObject py_has_rdseed(PyObject self, PyObject Py_UNUSED(ignored)) {
return PyBool_FromLong(cpuid_has_rdseed());
}
5. GIL release/entropy exhaustion race*
You do Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS then memcpy into buf. If another thread runs a GC and decides to resize the heap, buf is still valid because PyBytesObject is immovable. So this is fine. But if you ever switch to PyByteArray this pattern breaks. Document that PyBytes is required.

6. max_retries not validated
max_retries = 100 default is fine, but user can pass -1. Then while (retries--) becomes infinite loop. Check it:
if (max_retries < 0) {
PyErr_SetString(PyExc_ValueError, "max_retries must be >= 0");
return NULL;
}
Also consider max_retries == 0 means "try once". Is that what you want?

7. Missing static on module init for limited API
If you ever build with Py_LIMITED_API, PyModuleDef must be static but not const. Yours is fine. But PyInit_hwrng should be static if you don't export symbols. Not a bug, just hygiene.

8. Endianness assumption
You memcpy the uint64_t directly to bytes. On little-endian x86 this gives you LSB first. That's probably what you want for crypto, but if someone expects big-endian output this will surprise them. Document it: "bytes are native little-endian 64-bit words".

9. _mm_pause header
_mm_pause() is from <immintrin.h> which you included, but on MSVC it's also fine. However, on old GCC you might need <xmmintrin.h>. <immintrin.h> is the umbrella header on modern compilers, so you're ok. Just noting.

10. No check for PyBytes_AS_STRING macro
You're using PyBytes_AS_STRING which returns char*. CPython guarantees it's writable for newly created bytes objects, so ok. But if n_bytes is huge, PyBytes_New can fail with MemoryError before you even touch it. You handle if (!result) return NULL; so that's covered.

Summary: Critical fixes needed
1. Fix MSVC compile guard
2. Use uint64_t not unsigned long long, and use sizeof(uint64_t)
3. Fix METH_NOARGS signature
4. Validate max_retries >= 0
5. Handle 32-bit with _rdseed32_step or refuse to build

Everything else is correctness/defensive coding. As-is, this will SIGSEGV on 32-bit Python or throw a compile error on MSVC.

If that grabs too much junk, use this more aggressive version - it scrolls to top first and grabs everything:
async function copyAllChats(){
// Auto-scroll to load all history
for(let i=0;i<30;i++){
window.scrollTo(0,0);
await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,600));
if(window.scrollY===0) break;
}
window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight);

let out = "";
document.querySelectorAll('*').forEach(n=>{
if(n.children.length===0 && n.innerText && n.innerText.length>2){
// only leaf text nodes = actual messages
if(!out.includes(n.innerText)) out += n.innerText + "\n\n";
}
});
await navigator.clipboard.writeText(out);
console.log(out);
alert("Done - all chat copied");
}
copyAllChats();

// 1. This is the trick - it doesn't scrape the visible DOM.
// It injects into WhatsApp's own webpack store to get all msgs at once.
function getWhatsAppStore() {
// WhatsApp Web hides its data in webpack modules
